content.intro: This lesson studies Authentication and Route Access within Vue Router and Application Navigation. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Routing lets a Vue app behave like a multi-page product while remaining a single-page application in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Authentication and Route Access: Safe rendering and trust boundaries
content_blocks.alt_text: Safe rendering and trust boundaries diagram for lesson 78: Authentication and Route Access. Treat strings, URLs, and client state as untrusted → Escape text; validate URLs and payloads → Enforce access and sensitive decisions on the backend
content_blocks.caption: Security flow: untrusted values are rendered safely, while the server remains responsible for authorization and sensitive decisions.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Vue Router maps URLs to views and supports dynamic parameters, nested layouts, guards, lazy-loaded components, and navigation state. This lesson focuses on Authentication and Route Access. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Redirecting unauthenticated users
items.text: For Redirecting unauthenticated users, keep the URL as the addressable navigation state, use named route records when practical, and handle invalid parameters or failed navigation explicitly. A route guard improves navigation flow but does not replace backend access control.

items.title: Role-aware user interface navigation
items.text: For Role-aware user interface navigation, keep the URL as the addressable navigation state, use named route records when practical, and handle invalid parameters or failed navigation explicitly. A route guard improves navigation flow but does not replace backend access control.

items.title: Why frontend route guards do not replace backend authorization
items.text: For Why frontend route guards do not replace backend authorization, treat browser input and browser-held state as untrusted. Prefer Vue's escaped text interpolation for plain text, avoid compiling user-provided templates, and send authorization or sensitive decisions to a server that verifies them independently.

content_blocks.expected_output: A navigation to a route marked requiresAuth redirects to login if the UI auth state says no; this is not a substitute for server-side authorization.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This excerpt belongs after router and auth store setup. Validate permissions on protected API routes regardless of client navigation.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. content.task: Create a small example for “Authentication and Route Access” that applies “Public and private page patterns”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Public and private page patterns”.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
